title: Empty Rig
passages:
The impact wrench screamed as Rhea torqued the last brake relay bolt on ghost train 44. Hydraulic fluid wept from the fitting, hot and sharp on her gloves. She wiped it on her coverall thigh and checked the torque wrench readout. Green. Good.

"Four-four's clear for the morning push," she called down to the pit. Her voice bounced off the corrugated steel walls of Bay 2.

Bex leaned over the guardrail, clipboard glowing. The yard boss's face was a topography of oil stains and sleep deprivation. "Clear ain't signed. You know the drill. Three copies. One for the node, one for the rig, one for the archive in case the satellites forget we exist."

"The satellites don't forget. They just bill us for the reminder." Rhea unplugged the diagnostic lead from the rig's neck port. The connector clicked, final as a coffin latch. "Four-four's got seven thousand hours on the drivetrain. Her brakes are newer than your clipboard."

"Paperwork's the only thing keeps the Interior from eating us alive." Bex tapped the screen. "Sign. Then you can go count your brother's air cartridges again."

Rhea signed. The stylus dragged. Her thumb hovered over the confirm button a beat longer than necessary — sixty-one hours. Four hundred kilometers to Anza Node. The math didn't improve with staring.

"Done." She handed back the clipboard.

Bex didn't look up. "Miko's in Bay 6. Ballast detail. Try not to let her blow anything up before shift change."

"Miko blows things up *after* shift change. It's her thing." Rhea started for the personnel door, unzipping her coverall to the waist. The node's air tasted of diesel, ozone, and the particular dust that never quite settled.

Bay 6 yawned three hundred meters down the yard, a rectangle of sodium vapor cutting the twilight. Miko stood atop a pallet stack, forklift forks buried in a crate of ceramic ballast bricks. She moved with the lazy precision of someone who'd loaded ten thousand tons and expected to load ten thousand more. Her loader's slate — a ruggedized tablet strapped to her forearm — flickered with three different names. Rhea caught the edges: *Chen, Vasquez, Okonkwo*. Coast-bound tickets, all of them.

"Evening, Rhea," Miko called down without looking. "Bex still riding the paperwork pony?"

"Still riding. Still breathing." Rhea shielded her eyes against the glare. "How's the ballast?"

"Heavy. Boring. Exactly what I paid for." Miko tilted the crate, forks humming. "You heading out?"

"Shift's up in twenty. Ivo's holding at Anza. Sixty-one hours on his filters." The words came out flat. Practiced.

Miko paused. The forklift whined as she lowered the load. "Sixty-one's better than sixty. Better than zero."

"Yeah. It is."

The yard horn shattered the moment — three long blasts, the inbound signal. Rhea's head snapped toward the dispatch tower. Bay 4. The medical bay. Cold storage. The board at the tower's base showed nothing. No rig ID. No ETA. No consignee.

Bay 4's status light pulsed amber. Empty.

"Inbound to Bay 4," the automated voice droned, flat and indifferent. "Stand by for docking."

Miko's forklift went silent. She swung down from the cab, landing light on her boots. "That's weird. Medical rigs don't just *show up*."

"Nothing just shows up," Rhea said. Her hand found the diagnostic pouch at her belt. "Not at Kettering."

The amber light kept pulsing. Somewhere in the dark beyond the yard lights, something massive slowed. Engine note low. Tires on gravel.

Rhea went alone. That was her first mistake, though she wouldn't know it for a while.

Miko hung at the bay's mouth, and Rhea waved her off without turning — "Stay on the ballast" — and walked into the sodium light of Bay 4.

The rig sat dead center of the bay, parked square between the painted lines like it had been placed there by a hand that cared about neatness. A medical transport: a cab up front, and behind it a climate box, the insulated cargo section that holds its own temperature whether the world outside is baking or frozen. And inside that, behind a small fogged window, the pale outline of a life pod — a sealed bed unit that breathes for a person who can't. Air, warmth, fluids. Rhea had serviced a dozen of them. Never one that arrived without a sound.

Because there was no sound. No idle hum. No pumps. The cab's marker lights were dark. The thing had driven itself here and then stopped being alive.

"No consignee," she said to the empty bay. Her voice came back off the walls.

She pulled the manifest off the rig's flank port with her handheld — a diagnostic scanner, a rugged brick that read a vehicle's every system and told you what was wrong in plain words. She'd trusted that brick more than she trusted most people, and it had earned it.

The manifest scrolled. Cargo: nine hundred kilos, ceramic ballast. Destination: blank. Consignee: blank.

"Ballast," Rhea said. "You crossed the whole Interior full of rocks."

She walked the length of the climate box. The seals were the giveaway — tamper strips, thin plastic bands that snap the first time you open a hatch and can't be used twice, one on each door. Somebody had cut every one. Then, worse, replaced them. Hand-stamped. The serial numbers didn't match the rig's registry; she could see the crooked digits from a meter off, ink still wet at one edge. A person had knelt here in the dark with a stamp and lied to the truck.

The truck hadn't noticed. Trucks don't.

She keyed the diagnostic sweep and the brick filled green in her palm. Drivetrain: green. Climate: green, holding four degrees. Life support: green. Pod battery: green. Everything the machine could say about itself came back clean as a whistle, and that — the clean of it — was the only reason she believed any of it. The brick never lied. People lied. The truck was fine.

"Okay," she breathed. "What are you carrying."

The pod's window was fogged from the inside. Warm fog. Something in there was breathing.

Her stomach dropped through the concrete. Nine hundred kilos of ballast does not fog a window.

Rhea reached for the pod's manual release and stopped, because behind her boots crunched on the bay grit, unhurried, and a voice she knew chewed its way around a wad of gum.

"That's a med rig," Miko said, ambling out of the dark with her slate glowing on her forearm and her pack — when had she grabbed her pack? — slung over one shoulder. "A cold one. No route ping, no board entry, and it parked itself neat as Sunday." She stopped beside Rhea, tilted her head at the fogged window, and blew a pink bubble that popped in the quiet. "So. What's in the box?"

Rhea popped the cover off the pod's manual release — a hinged steel plate with a red lever under it, for when the power dies and somebody has to open a bed with their hands — and pulled.

The pod let go of its pressure in a long sigh. Cold rolled out over her boots, four degrees of it, smelling of clean plastic and somebody else's blood.

"Charming," Miko said. "I was hoping for rocks."

"Ballast doesn't fog glass."

The lid came up in three stages, each one a clack of gas struts, and Rhea stood over a man about fifty with a gray stubble and a jaw gone slack. Gray coverall, unmarked except for a cargo-loader's patch on the left shoulder — the iron-on badge that says you're rated to lash and load, the only thing that stands between you and the clinic when a rig shifts wrong. A syringe driver was taped into the crook of his arm, a little pump the size of a deck of cards that pushes a drug in at a set rate for as long as its battery holds. His eyes moved under the lids. Breathing, slow and regular. Sedated to the roof of his skull.

Where the name tape goes, there was nothing. Not blank fabric — a rectangle of unfaded cloth with the stitching holes still in it, the shape of a name that somebody had cut out with a blade while he was under.

"Pod chart?" Rhea said.

The headwall screen held a chart slot, the log a pod keeps on its own: who is inside, what it has pumped into them, vitals by the minute, who signed them in. It was empty. Not wiped. Never started. Whoever put him in had known enough to skip the only part that gets recorded.

"Okay," Miko said. Her gum had gone still. "So he's a person, not ballast. That's a load of nine hundred kilos I could have skipped."

"Help me find a wristband."

"He's got a band."

She meant the cargo band. Two inches of ratchet strap, the kind loaders cinch down a pallet with, pulled through the pod's side rail and locked with the handle folded flat. The band went around his left wrist. Not across his chest. Not his ankles. One wrist, to the rail, cinched hard enough that the hand below it had gone the color of a bruise.

Rhea put two fingers under the strap and eased the ratchet a quarter turn. Color came back into the fingers.

"Somebody was careful," she said. "Careful enough to skip the chart and careful enough to keep the arm where he couldn't reach the release."

"Battery?"

Rhea checked the brick. Pod battery, green, 29:00. Twenty-nine hours of air and heat and pump for a man with no name. Ivo had sixty-one. This man had twenty-nine, and no chart, and nowhere to be.

"Twenty-nine," she said.

Miko crouched, tilted her head, read the stencil on the strap. Loaders stencil their bands: bay, shift, load number, so a strap that turns up on the wrong rig can be traced back to the hands that cinched it.

And then Miko stopped chewing.

"That's Bay 4," she said. "Shift two."

"This shift."

"This shift, Rhea. The one that ends in eighteen minutes." Miko straightened up, and she didn't look at the man anymore. She looked at the yard lights beyond the bay mouth, where two dozen people were about to clock out. "Somebody in this yard knelt down in our medical bay with a stamp in their hand and put a person in a box and drove him here to park."

Rhea's mouth was dry. The brick in her hand said everything was fine, and the brick was right, and the brick had been lied to by somebody with a stamp and a shift number and a key to Bay 4.

On the headwall, the battery number rolled over. 28:59.

PASSAGE ends.
